newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian satellite launch to open new cosmodrome.
newsitem.headline: Russian satellite launch to open new cosmodrome.

text.p: Russia will stage the maiden launch from its new cosmodrome in the Far East on Tuesday when a military satellite blasts into orbit aboard a modified SS-25 ballistic missile, space officials said on Monday.

The launch from the Svobodny cosmodrome, still being built on a former strategic nuclear missile base on the Siberian taiga 860 km (540 miles) west of Khabarovsk, will take place despite protests from local authorities and environmentalists.

Colonel Sergei Gorbunov, a spokesman for Russia's Military Space Forces, said Svobodny -- the name means "Free" -- would become the main launch site for the commercial satellites Moscow is banking on to fund its financially troubled space industry.

The 87-kg (191 lb) Zeya military satellite, whose precise function has not been disclosed, will blast off at 0200 GMT on Tuesday aboard a Start booster rocket -- in effect a modified SS-25 Topol (Poplar) missile originally designed to carry nuclear payloads to North American cities.
Ironically a U.S. satellite may be the next to be launched from Svobodny and other western ventures, now the Russian space industry's main paymasters, will follow.

Russian officials believe that the construction of Svobodny, on the same latitude as the main Soviet space centre Baikonur in now independent Kazakhstan, should allow much more effective launches than from Russia's two other sites in northern Russia.
They believe Svobodny will reduce Russia's dependence on Baikonur, whose maintenance and rent conditions are the source of unending squabbles between Moscow and Almaty.
"This will allow Russia to add to the full independence of its space programme," Gorbunov said.
The space industry, once the pride of the Soviet Union, has fallen on hard times since the superpower collapsed in 1991.
Several flights have been delayed because of cash shortages, while a fire on the ageing orbital station Mir last week did little to bolster global confidence in Moscow's space programme.

Interfax news agency said a U.S. satellite, Early Bird, would be launched in the third quarter of 1997, followed later this year by a British satellite on a Rokot (Thunder) boosted rocket and a Swedish satellite in 1998.
Gorbunov said that there were no immediate plans to transfer launches of manned space flights from Baikonur to Svobodny.
He said solid-fuel rockets like the Start presented no danger to the environment around Svobodny but admitted that parts of its boosters would fall to earth after launch.
Environmentalists and local authorities in neighbouring areas of Siberia take a rather different view.
Itar-Tass news agency said protesters took to the streets on Monday in Yakutsk, capital of the diamond-rich ethnic republic of Sakha-Yakutia, north of the new cosmodrome.

The protesters, with the apparent support of the local authorities, marched through the ice-bound town carrying banners reading "Down With Rocket Dumping!", "Down With The New Baikonur!" and "Let's Preserve Our Environment".
Tass said Yakutia government officials had earlier sent a letter to the Defence Ministry saying they doubted the environmental and technical safety of the Start rocket.
The Yakutia authorities have threatened to scrap a 1996 agreement allowing rocket components to fall on their territory if Tuesday's launch goes ahead without their consent.
